ending: After a lifetime of seeking, Siddhartha reaches enlightenment not through any teaching but through his own long experience of the world and, above all, through listening to the river with Vasudeva, in whose voice he hears all of existence flowing together as one. Having endured the loss of his son, who fled back to the town, he lets his suffering dissolve into acceptance and love for the whole of life. Vasudeva, his work complete, walks into the forest and leaves Siddhartha as the ferryman and keeper of the crossing. In the final chapter his old friend Govinda, grown old and still restless in his search, comes to the river and does not at first recognize him. Siddhartha tells him that wisdom cannot be conveyed in words and that time is an illusion in which everything already exists at once, and he asks Govinda to kiss his forehead. Doing so, Govinda beholds a flowing vision of countless faces and forms merging into a single unity and a serene, all-embracing love, and he weeps, sensing that his friend has found what they both spent their lives pursuing.
in_short: Siddhartha, a Brahmin's son in ancient India, leaves home with his friend Govinda to seek enlightenment, first as a wandering ascetic and then in the presence of the Buddha, whom he admires but refuses to follow, convinced that wisdom cannot be taught. Turning instead to worldly experience, he crosses a river, learns love from the courtesan Kamala, and grows rich in trade, only to sicken of greed and pleasure and, in despair, nearly drown himself in that same river. Renewed, he stays to become a ferryman beside the wise Vasudeva, learning to listen to the river. Kamala, now a pilgrim, dies at the crossing and leaves Siddhartha their young son, whose bitterness and eventual flight teach him the pain of love and attachment. Through the river's voice Siddhartha finally attains the peace and unity he sought, and Vasudeva departs. Years later Govinda, still searching, meets him again, and Siddhartha shares a wordless vision of the oneness of all things.

recaps.text: Siddhartha, the brilliant son of a Brahmin, is admired by everyone yet inwardly restless, certain that the rituals and teachings of his upbringing cannot give him the peace he craves. With his devoted friend Govinda, he leaves home to join the Samanas, wandering ascetics, and for years he practices fasting, self-denial, and the discipline of thinking, waiting, and going without, mastering the mortification of the body and the will. But he concludes that asceticism, too, is only another escape and cannot bring true understanding. Hearing of the enlightened teacher Gotama, the Buddha, the friends go to see him. Govinda is won over and joins the Buddha's order, but Siddhartha, though he recognizes the teacher's perfect serenity and the truth of his doctrine, declines to become a follower. He reasons that enlightenment is a lived experience no teaching can hand over. Parting from Govinda, Siddhartha awakens to a new resolve: to stop fleeing the world and instead learn from it directly, embracing his own senses and self.

Siddhartha crosses a great river, ferried by a humble boatman in whom he senses a quiet depth, and enters a town to learn the life of the senses he has always denied. There he meets Kamala, a beautiful and worldly courtesan, who agrees to teach him the art of love if he can bring her wealth and fine things. To win them, Siddhartha takes work with the merchant Kamaswami and proves shrewd at trade, growing rich while treating business almost as a game and keeping, at first, an inner detachment. Over the years, though, the world claims him: he acquires property, gambles recklessly, drinks, and chases pleasure, and the calm he brought from his years of discipline slowly erodes. He comes to feel trapped in the very greed and craving he once scorned, sick at heart and spiritually hollow, until the emptiness of his rich, restless life becomes unbearable.

In despair, Siddhartha abandons his wealth and Kamala and wanders back to the river, so disgusted with himself that he comes to the edge of drowning. At that lowest point the sacred syllable Om rises from within him, and he falls into a deep, healing sleep by the water. He wakes renewed, feeling reborn, and finds that Govinda, now a wandering monk, had watched over him without knowing him. Choosing to stay by the river, Siddhartha becomes the apprentice and companion of Vasudeva, the gentle ferryman, and takes up the simple work of carrying travelers across. Vasudeva teaches him to listen, and from the ever-flowing water Siddhartha begins to learn its lessons, that time is not real and that all things are connected, finding in this quiet life a peace that his years of seeking and indulgence never gave him.

Kamala, now a follower of the Buddha, comes on pilgrimage toward the dying teacher, bringing with her a young son, Siddhartha's child, whom he never knew he had. Bitten by a snake near the river, she dies in Siddhartha's care, and he is left to raise the boy. But the child, spoiled by his former life of comfort, is angry and grieving and despises the poor, simple existence of the ferry and the patient father who loves him. Siddhartha's love binds him painfully to the boy, and he suffers the wound of attachment he had never truly known before, until the son finally runs away back to the town. Aching and unable to let go, Siddhartha at last turns to the river once more, and listening to its many voices flow together into a single sound, he releases his grief and attains a profound peace and sense of unity. Recognizing that his own task is finished, Vasudeva takes leave of him and departs into the forest.

Many years later Govinda, grown old and still searching for the peace that has eluded him, comes to the river crossing and does not recognize the ferryman as his boyhood friend. When Siddhartha reveals himself, Govinda asks what wisdom or teaching guides him. Siddhartha explains that true wisdom cannot be put into words or passed from one person to another, that its opposite is always equally true, and that time is an illusion in which every thing and every possibility already exists together in a single eternal moment. He speaks of loving the world as it is rather than judging or fleeing it. Unable fully to grasp this in words, Govinda accepts Siddhartha's invitation to kiss his forehead, and in that instant he sees a vast, flowing vision of countless faces, creatures, and forms merging endlessly into one another within a serene and boundless love. Overcome, Govinda bows before his friend, sensing that Siddhartha has reached the very enlightenment they both spent their lives pursuing.
